tip: Bare kerja is any work; add -nya and it's this specific one: kerjanya juga berat = the work is also heavy. -nya often does the job of English 'the'.
Sungkan isn't plain hesitation – it's the feeling of not wanting to impose on someone. Jangan sungkan bertanya = don't hold back out of politeness, just ask.
Saling before a verb makes it mutual: membantu = help, saling membantu = help each other. No extra 'each other' word needed after the verb.
Ke-...-an marks accidents: tinggal = stay behind, ketinggalan = got left behind – nobody did it on purpose. Same move in ketiduran (accidentally fell asleep).
The -an ending turns an action into its thing: antre = to queue up, antrean = the line itself. Same trick in makan – makanan (food), minum – minuman (drink).
Stick -an on a time word to get a 'per' word: hari – harian (daily), minggu – mingguan (weekly), bulan – bulanan (monthly). Sewa harian = daily rental.
Pulang pergi is literally 'go-home go' – the trip home gets named first. Tiket pulang pergi = a round-trip ticket, often shortened to PP on booking sites.
Salah slots before almost any verb to mean doing it wrong: salah beli = bought the wrong one, salah paham = misunderstood, salah sambung = dialed the wrong number.
Adding -kan aims the action at a beneficiary: membuat teh = made tea, membuatkan kami teh = made tea for us. The person served comes right after the verb.
Kabar is the noun 'news'; the -i ending turns it into a verb: kabari kami = send us word. Indonesian builds verbs straight from nouns this way all the time.
Masing-masing sits after the noun and covers 'their own' by itself: kota masing-masing = their own cities – no separate word for 'their' needed.
Deadlines use superlatives: paling lambat, literally 'most late', means at the latest – paling lambat tanggal lima = by the fifth. Paling cepat works for 'at the earliest'.
Saling makes almost any verb mutual: saling membantu = help each other, saling kenal = know each other, saling percaya = trust each other.
Menyampaikan comes from sampai (arrive, reach): to voice something is to make it reach people. Menyampaikan pendapat = get your opinion across.
Lipat means fold, so dua kali lipat = 'two times folded', like English twofold. It scales: tiga kali lipat = tripled. Naik dua kali lipat = doubled.
Doubling an adjective softens it into a gradual manner: pelan = slow, pelan-pelan = little by little. Pelan-pelan rasa takutnya hilang = the fear slowly faded.
Indonesian pairs 'different' with 'with', not 'from': berbeda dengan iklim di Jakarta. Berbeda dari isn't wrong, but dengan is what you'll hear.
Pahitnya kayak obat sounds like family chat – kayak lives in relaxed speech. The moment you write anything formal (an email, a report), it becomes seperti.
Lengket seperti perangko – stuck like a stamp – is the set image for two people who are never apart. Lengket alone is the sticky feel of rice or glue.
Ter- marks what happens with nobody intending it: tertinggal = got left behind by accident. The package ternyata tertinggal – it turned out left behind, no one chose that.
Everyday speech puts the lost item in charge: kunci gudang itu belum ketemu = the warehouse key hasn't turned up. Ketemu is casual – formal writing uses ditemukan.
Once antre (queue up) takes -an it's a full noun: antrean panjang itu – it takes an adjective, takes itu, and stands as the subject of the sentence.
Doubling a verb makes it aimless and unhurried: melihat = look at, melihat-lihat = browse with no target. Hanya mau melihat-lihat = just looking, the shop answer.
Berjualan is selling as your trade, not one transaction: nenek dulu berjualan kue = grandma used to sell cakes for a living. To sell one specific thing, use menjual.
Double a time word and it stretches into a process: lama = a long while, lama-lama = over time, bit by bit. Lama-lama dia belajar memasak = over time she learned to cook.
Gurih is the savory richness of coconut milk, broth, and fried things – a core taste word English has no exact match for. Bumbu kacang yang gurih = savory peanut sauce.
Kenyal is the prized springy-bouncy bite: baksonya kenyal is a compliment. The opposite, lembek (mushy), is a failed bakso.
Kecap is soy sauce, not ketchup – kecap manis is the sweet, syrupy kind brushed on grilled chicken. English actually borrowed 'ketchup' from this Malay word.
Ayam kampung is literally 'village chicken' – free-range birds that roam the kampung, pricier but lebih gurih. Ordinary farmed chicken is ayam negeri or broiler.
Diungkep is a specific kitchen step: simmered slowly in the spice paste so bumbunya meresap. Direbus is just boiling in water – it wouldn't get the seasoning in.
English 'rice' splits in two: beras is the raw grain you buy, nasi is cooked rice on the plate. Lontong starts from beras, then cooks inside the banana leaf.
Pun attaches after the word it stresses: level lima pun = even level five. Paired with masih kurang it builds the common 'even X still isn't enough' shape.
Warung custom: you eat first and settle up after. Bayarnya nanti saja di kasir = just pay later at the register – no one expects payment before the food.
Boleh minta + the thing is the all-purpose polite request – no 'may I have' verb chain needed: boleh minta password wifi-nya. The closing ya softens it further.
Ngecas puts the casual nge- prefix on the borrowed root cas (from 'charge'). Loanwords take Indonesian prefixes freely – and every generation says ngecas HP.
Even a borrowed root takes the passive di-: cas (charge) becomes dicas = gets charged. HP saya dicas = my phone was charged – no 'was' word needed.
Tinggal usually means 'live, stay', but before an amount it means what's left: tinggal sepuluh persen = only ten percent remaining. Context picks the meaning.
Pengeluaran is built on keluar (go out): expenses are literally 'the going-out' of money. Its mirror is pemasukan, income – money coming in (masuk).
Doubling turns a one-off into an on-and-off: putus = cut off, putus-putus = keeps cutting out. Sering putus-putus (often cutting out) is the classic bad-connection complaint.
English loans work as verbs with nothing added: kami video call – no melakukan, no verb ending. Same with meeting, chat, and upload in office talk.
Mematikan is literally 'make dead': mati (dead) + me-...-kan. Turning off the mikrofon means killing it – the same logic English uses in 'kill the lights'.
Gambar selamat pagi – flowery good-morning images – are a daily ritual in Indonesian family chat groups, sent most faithfully by om dan tante.
Belum tentu is literally 'not yet certain': belum tentu benar = not necessarily true. Indonesian prefers belum (not yet) where English says a flat 'not'.
Kampung halaman is a fixed pair meaning your family's hometown – where you're from, not just any village. Plain kampung can be any village or neighborhood.
Mengunggah = upload and mengunduh = download are near-twins that are easy to swap. Casual speech dodges the problem: people say upload and download as-is.
